title: Steadfastness in the Cross of Christ
english: And yet Paul cries out, 'Be steadfast, immovable!' But the Lord himself, in his most approachable and persuasive manner, sets the highest value on those who possess anything, only to meet with slander. He draws a boundary against the disease of turning away.

For he said of certain ones, 'They loved to move their feet and did not spare themselves, and God did not approve in them.' For what is firmly and immovably established toward anything useful is safe and inviolable. Indeed, the blood of animals is brought forth, and so on.

But there are also many other words about these matters; however, let them pass by now because of their multitude. Nevertheless, Christ died according to the flesh, that he might cleanse us by his own blood.
Therefore we go forth to him. Let us then bear his reproach, that is, the cross on our behalf. Thus he also said, 'Whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me.'
translator_notes: The Greek text begins mid-sentence at [p1] καίτοι Παύλου μὲν διακεκραγότος, so the opening participle is translated as a fragment.
The phrase κ.τ.λ. at [p3] and [p6] is retained as 'etc.' in the translation, following the source.
The final clause at [p8] ends mid-sentence with τὸ, so the English rendering ends with 'the' to reflect the cutoff; no completion is attempted.

title: The Union of the Word and the Saints
english: …It seems to think outside the gate, outside the world; for wanting to follow Christ unsettles our worldly life.

But the one who does good and is in communion is accepted by God, who rewards each according to their works, and says, 'Come, inherit the kingdom prepared for you, for I was hungry and you gave me food to eat' (Matt 25:34-35), and the following, how God is thus called by the pure voice of the saints, while accepting the sacrifices of those who do good, repaying each with the due reward, and admitting the chorus of the saints into the kingdom of heaven.

Paul calls the Son God; for if He is indeed the one who drives all creation toward judgment, and repays each according to their works, accepting those who do good to their neighbor and saying, 'Come, inherit the kingdom prepared for you, for I was hungry and you gave me food to eat' (Matt 25:34-35).

If it were said that the only-begotten Word of God happened to be united to the flesh by hypostasis, we do not say that any confusion of the two natures has occurred, but rather that the Word is understood to be united to the flesh while the other remains as it is.

'Those who think themselves wise have become foolish' (1 Cor 3:19); for they, having denied the two natures from one another and showing each part of us to be an incompatible stranger, say that the union exists only in persons, as if it were in mere agreement, common purpose, and the impulses of wills.

According to that, perhaps, what is written in the acts of the holy apostles (Acts 4:32), that 'the heart and the soul of the multitude of those who believed were one.' For each of those who believed, insofar as they were divided from the others by the logic of their own hypostasis, yet reached a common purpose and unity of faith, is said to have one soul and one heart; do they, then, acknowledge the unity of persons in this same way?
And not yet do we say that the nature of the Word of God is circumscribed in the human body, for the divine is incomprehensible.

Furthermore, it proceeds: one will see the human being completely in Christ, according to the logic of His own nature; and similarly, the Word born from God is seen as perfect; yet only one Christ and Son is confessed from both…
translator_notes: The text begins and ends mid-sentence; '…' indicates these fragments.
The clause 'καὶ λέγων' was missing from the previous draft and has been integrated into the description of God's actions.
The phrase 'καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς' (and the following) refers to the subsequent arguments regarding the saints' voices and sacrifices.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in Hebraeos u08 rem mid

title: Incarnation of the Logos
english: The union of natures is not merely a matter of the union of persons, but rather the natures are gathered into one, ineffably and beyond reason, as God himself has known.

We do not say that there is a confusion or disruption of the natures, as if the nature of the Logos were changed into that of man, or the human into that of the Logos, but rather that each nature remains within its own limit.
The union has been realized by the Logos dwelling bodily in the temple born of the virgin.
If anyone claims that the union is only of persons and completely separates the natures from each other, they stray from the straight path, as Cyril notes in his interpretation.
We see the one Christ, who is God incarnate, dying bodily for sin, so that by the sprinkling of his own blood he may wholly sanctify the Church, and remaining again impassible in his divinity.
As Cyril explains in his interpretation of the pros Hebraeous epistle, if he has perfected us by water and Spirit, then he must act both divinely and humanly at once, being the same one who exists.
It is a mystery that happened ineffably and beyond mind, that divinity and humanity were united, and though the natures are distinct, yet there is one and only Son from both.

Even if the natures were diverse and unequal to one another, and ran together into unity, there is still one and only Son from both, who is truly possessed of a rational soul and is the temple united to the Logos.

As Cyril notes, it was not a bare man, one of us, who could complete the energy of the according-to-nature life, but rather, as the most holy Paul says, it was by the grace of God that the body of the Logos, who became incarnate for us, tasted death, in order that the work of abolishing death might not be attributed to the earthly body, but rather to the Logos who is united to it and subsists alongside it.
The most holy Paul says, 'by the grace of God' (Hebrews 2:9), indicating that it was God's grace that allowed the Logos to taste death for the salvation of all.
translator_notes: The Greek text begins mid-sentence and ends mid-thought; all edge fragments are translated literally without completion.
The phrase 'pros Hebraeous' preserves the original Greek form of the epistle title.
The numeral '423' in the Greek text appears to be an OCR artifact or folio marker, not part of the original wording; it has been omitted from translation.
The final '25' in brackets appears to be a standalone digit, likely a folio or section number; it has been omitted as non-content.
The Greek text contains no explicit scripture citations, but rather allusions to biblical concepts and quotations, such as 'by the grace of God' (Hebrews 2:9).
